alt: The input text is split into tokens. The first two tokens are the row and column counts, read with int(). The next r tokens are the rows, sliced off the front of the list one row at a time, and each becomes one row of the grid.

steps.caption: `sys.stdin.read().split()` cuts the input at whitespace into 5 tokens: the two counts, then one token per row. The grid on the right is what the row tokens will become.
`r = int(data[0])` reads the first token, 3. The board has 3 rows.
`c = int(data[1])` reads the second token, 4. Every row has 4 columns.
`data[2:2 + r]` is `data[2:5]`: exactly the 3 tokens after the counts. Each one is a whole row, because a row has no spaces inside it.
`grid[0]` is `data[2]`, the string `..##`. Its 4 characters fill row 0 of the grid.
`grid[1]` is `data[3]`, the string `#...`. Its 4 characters fill row 1 of the grid.
`grid[2]` is `data[4]`, the string `....`. Its 4 characters fill row 2 of the grid.
The grid holds 3 rows of 4 characters. `grid[2][3]` is `'.'`, the last cell of the last row. Scanning this grid, as count_marks.py does, finds 3 marks.
